title: The LPG Model (New Economic Policy)
tagline: The three words of economic reform, each defined and judged by its positive impact on the Indian economy.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original BoardPrep study material written against the CISCE ICSE Economics syllabus registered in this subject’s baseline (the 2026-27 session syllabus as reproduced by Shaalaa and Jagran Josh; the official cisce.org PDFs were not retrievable). Every question and answer is original practice, no board examination paper was consulted, and no figure is presented as an official statistic.

overview.intro: The syllabus’s sixth unit begins with the model that reshaped the Indian economy, and it asks for a narrow, examinable thing: the meaning of each of the three terms and the positive impact of each on the Indian economy. This chapter gives both, in order. A short opening explains the context the reforms answered — an economy of licences, reserved sectors and closed trade whose shortages and stagnation made change unavoidable — because meaning is clearer against the problem it solved. Then each word gets its own lesson: liberalisation as the removal of controls on firms, privatisation as the reduction of the state’s role in production, globalisation as India’s integration with world markets. Each lesson states the meaning precisely, then itemises the positive impacts separately, since the examination wants impact and not merely definition. The chapter closes with the three as one package — because in practice they arrived together and reinforce one another — while keeping each term’s contribution distinct enough to answer a standalone question.

learningOutcomes: Explain the context in which the LPG model was adopted.
Define liberalisation and state its positive impacts on the Indian economy.
Define privatisation and state its positive impacts on the Indian economy.
Define globalisation and state its positive impacts on the Indian economy.
Show how the three reforms reinforce one another as a package.

blocks.text: For its first four decades India ran a controlled economy: a firm needed a government licence to start, to expand or to change what it made; a fixed list reserved many industries for the public sector; imports faced heavy duties and quotas so that foreign goods arrived only in small numbers and at high prices; and capital, foreign exchange and prices were administered rather than market-set. The intentions were sound — protecting infant industry, conserving foreign exchange, directing investment towards national priorities — but the accumulated effects were not. Licence controls removed the discipline of competition, so firms competed for permissions rather than for customers, quality stagnated and consumers waited years for goods that scarcity kept expensive. The public sector’s reserved list concentrated investment in plants that faced no market test, and losses could continue indefinitely because failure was not permitted. Closed trade kept domestic industry from the pressure that rewards efficiency, and by 1991 a balance-of-payments crisis — foreign exchange down to weeks of imports — forced the issue. The LPG model was the answer: liberalisation to release the entrepreneurial energy that licensing had frozen, privatisation to make the state’s role selective and the public sector answer to performance, and globalisation to import competition, capital and technology. The three names are one response to one diagnosis — an economy that had chosen efficiency’s intentions without its mechanisms.

items: Licence controls: permissions replaced competition, so firms lobbied regulators instead of serving buyers.
Reserved public sector: investment without market discipline, and losses financed indefinitely.
Closed trade: no external competition to punish inefficiency or reward quality.
The 1991 trigger: foreign exchange down to weeks of imports forced stabilisation and reform together.
LPG as one diagnosis: release enterprise (L), sharpen ownership (P), import discipline (G).

blocks.text: Liberalisation means the removal or relaxation of government controls over economic activity — industrial licensing was abolished for most industries, the areas reserved for the public sector were narrowed, quotas and tariffs on imports were cut, foreign investment was permitted in more sectors, and firms gained freedom in pricing, capacity and expansion without seeking prior permission. The positive impacts follow directly from each released control. Freed from licence approvals, firms could expand capacity and enter new lines in response to demand, so industrial output grew and shortages — the queues and waiting lists of the licence era — ended. Opening to imports and foreign investment brought competition into markets where a domestic firm had faced none; competition forced prices down and quality up, and the consumer, previously a supplicant, became a chooser. Access to foreign capital and technology modernised industry — plants could buy equipment and know-how instead of reinventing both, raising productivity. Freedom for Indian firms to import and to invest abroad widened their own horizons: exports grew, and Indian companies learned to compete abroad rather than only at home. And a more predictable policy environment — rules applied to all rather than permissions granted to some — attracted investment that administration had previously deterred. The impacts are best remembered as the consumer’s and the producer’s sides of one change: what control removed, competition restored.

Privatisation means reducing the role of the government in the ownership and management of industry — disinvestment of government equity in public-sector undertakings, the opening of reserved areas to private firms, and, where a public unit continues, its operation with commercial rather than administrative discipline. In the Indian form the state did not sell everything; it stepped back from being the default producer, keeping a strategic core while letting the market run the rest. The positive impacts are efficiency-side. Competition from private entrants forced public-sector units to cut costs and improve service — a telephone department that had made subscribers wait now faced alternatives and could not. Disinvestment brought professional management and capital into firms whose boards had answered to departments rather than to markets, so decision-making followed customers and performance instead of procedure. New entrants into formerly reserved areas multiplied output, employment and choice in sectors like telecommunications, automobiles and consumer goods. The government’s burden of bailing out loss-making units fell, freeing budget resources for infrastructure, health and education — expenditure shifted from propping up firms to building the ground they stand on. And the discipline of the stock market and of private shareholders made performance visible in a way departmental accounting never was. The honest boundary: privatisation’s gains depend on regulation — a private monopoly without oversight can replace an inefficient department with an expensive one — which is why the reform’s positive impact is claimed for competition introduced, not for private ownership alone.

items.meaning: Reducing the government’s role in production through disinvestment and the opening of reserved sectors.
items.context: The state keeps a strategic core and lets markets run the rest.

items.meaning: Sale of part or all of the government’s equity in a public-sector undertaking.
items.context: Disinvestment brings capital and professional management into state firms.

items.meaning: Industries the state reserved exclusively for public enterprises.
items.context: Narrowing the reserved list let private firms enter and compete.

items.meaning: Running an enterprise by profit, cost and customer response rather than by administrative rule.
items.context: Commercial discipline is what privatisation aims to impose on surviving public firms.

blocks.text: Globalisation is the integration of a country’s economy with the world economy — freer flow of goods, services, capital, technology and people across borders, so that producers, consumers and investors operate in one connected market rather than in protected national ones. For India it meant cutting tariffs, abolishing quotas, welcoming foreign direct investment and portfolio capital, allowing Indian firms to source and sell globally, and accepting the disciplines of international trade. The positive impacts are wide. Foreign investment brought capital that domestic savings could not cover alone, along with technology and management practice transferred with it — joint ventures introduced production methods and quality standards that raised the productivity of Indian industry around them. Consumers gained choice and price: imported goods and competitive domestic goods became cheaper and better, and the variety of a global market arrived in place of the shortages of a closed one. Exports expanded — Indian software, textiles, pharmaceuticals and services found world markets — which earned foreign exchange, created employment in tradable sectors and tied Indian firms to global demand. Integration also discipline: exposure to world prices forced efficiency on firms that had never faced it, and the inflow of investment reflected confidence in a stable, open economy. Finally, globalisation connected India’s human capital to global demand directly, as services could be exported without moving people — a structural change whose employment effects the country is still absorbing. The three reforms, taken together, form the package: liberalisation freed the domestic firm, globalisation placed it on the world stage, and privatisation reshaped who stands beside it at home.

items: Meaning: integration through freer flow of goods, services, capital, technology and people.
Capital: foreign investment supplements domestic savings and carries technology with it.
Consumers: more choice, lower prices, better quality — the shortage economy ended.
Exports: world markets for software, textiles, pharmaceuticals — earnings and employment.
Efficiency: world-price exposure disciplines firms that never faced competition.
Package: liberalisation frees the firm, globalisation gives it the world stage, privatisation reshapes the domestic field.

blocks.text: The three terms are separable in a definition answer and inseparable in practice. Liberalisation without globalisation would have freed Indian firms from domestic controls while leaving them shielded from world competition — internal liberty without external test. Globalisation without liberalisation would have opened borders while the licence regime still gated entry, so imports would have arrived but domestic capacity could not respond. Privatisation without either would have changed owners without changing behaviour — a public monopoly sold becomes a private monopoly still untested. Together they interlock: licensing abolition let firms expand, foreign investment supplied the capital and technology to fill that capacity, and competition — domestic from new entrants, external from imports — determined which expansions were worth making. The effects compound in the same direction: lower tariffs force quality up, freer entry multiplies choice, and a state freed from running firms redirects resources towards the infrastructure and skills that all three reforms need to perform. For examinations the structure stays simple and effective — define the term, give its positive impacts as itemised mechanisms, and keep the package paragraph as the closing synthesis that shows the three were one policy rather than three unrelated decisions. Judged as a whole, the model’s record is the transformation of an economy from shortage to choice, from permission to competition, from isolation to integration — with the continuing tasks of inequality, employment quality and regulation stated honestly alongside.

items.text: A car buyer in 1991 waited years for one model at a fixed price; a decade later several manufacturers competed on price, features and service.
items.note: The package at the showroom: capacity freed, investment admitted, competition deciding.

items.text: A software firm formed under liberalisation exports services globally, earning foreign exchange without shipping goods.
items.note: Globalisation of services — integration without moving a single container.

keyPoints: LPG answers one diagnosis: licence discipline replaced by market discipline.
Liberalisation = removal of controls: licensing, quotas, reserved areas, price and capacity rules.
Liberalisation’s impacts: expansion without approval ends shortages; competition cuts price and raises quality; imports bring capital and technology.
Privatisation = reducing the state’s role: disinvestment, opening reserved sectors, commercial discipline for surviving public firms.
Privatisation’s impacts: efficiency under competition, professional management, multiplied output and choice, budget freed for infrastructure.
Privatisation’s gains require competition and regulation — ownership alone is not the mechanism.
Globalisation = integration through freer flows of goods, services, capital, technology and people.
Globalisation’s impacts: capital and technology inflows, consumer choice and price, exports and employment, efficiency under world prices.
The three are separable in definition and inseparable in practice — each needs the others to work.
The honest record: shortage became choice, permission became competition, isolation became integration — with inequality and employment quality as continuing tasks.
examFocus: Define the term first, in one sentence, before listing impacts — definition and impact carry separate marks.
Give positive impacts as mechanisms: control removed → what became possible → impact.
Keep liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation impacts in their own columns — never blurred into one list.
Use consumer-side impacts (price, quality, choice) alongside producer-side (capacity, technology, exports).
State the 1991 context briefly for meaning questions — reform reads clearly against the shortage economy.
Add the package paragraph as synthesis, and the regulation caveat where balance is asked for.
Never present impacts as costless: honesty about continuing tasks earns, not loses, credit.
Concrete examples — cars, telephones, software exports — turn abstract impacts into visible ones.

options: Removal or relaxation of government controls over economic activity
Sale of all public-sector enterprises to private owners
Increase in the number of industrial licences
questions.answer: Removal or relaxation of government controls over economic activity
questions.explanation: Liberalisation is about controls: licensing, quotas, reserved sectors and administered prices are relaxed so firms and markets can decide. Ownership (privatisation) and borders (globalisation) are the other two terms.
questions.commonMistake: Absorbing privatisation into liberalisation — freeing firms from rules and selling state firms are separate terms with separate marks.

questions.prompt: Which is a positive impact of globalisation on the Indian economy?
options: Inflow of foreign capital and technology alongside wider consumer choice
End of exports to world markets
questions.answer: Inflow of foreign capital and technology alongside wider consumer choice
questions.explanation: Integration brings investment that domestic savings cannot cover, carries technology with it, and exposes consumers to competitive goods — all prescribed positive impacts. The other options describe reversing globalisation.
questions.commonMistake: Citing only consumer benefits; capital and technology inflow is the producer-side impact exams expect too.

questions.prompt: Privatisation in the Indian context primarily involves:
options: Reducing the government’s role in production through disinvestment and opening reserved sectors
questions.answer: Reducing the government’s role in production through disinvestment and opening reserved sectors
questions.explanation: Privatisation steps the state back from being the default producer — selling equity, narrowing reserved areas and imposing commercial discipline — while a strategic core may remain public.
questions.commonMistake: Reading it as total sale of everything: the Indian form is a reduced, selective state role, not the disappearance of the public sector.

questions.prompt: Why did industrial licensing become a target of reform?
options: It made firms compete for permissions rather than for customers, so quality stagnated
It raised the prices of exported goods
It guaranteed employment to all graduates
questions.answer: It made firms compete for permissions rather than for customers, so quality stagnated
questions.explanation: Under licence controls, the constraint on a firm was regulatory approval, not market demand — so effort went into permissions and quotas, and consumers faced shortage and poor quality rather than competition.
questions.commonMistake: Blaming high taxation — the licence regime’s core failure was the discipline it replaced, not the levy it imposed.

questions.prompt: Complete: the LPG model stands for ________ , meaning removal of controls, ________ , meaning a reduced role of the state in production, and globalisation, meaning integration with the world economy.
questions.explanation: The three terms in order: liberalisation frees domestic activity from controls, privatisation reshapes ownership, globalisation opens the economy to the world — one package with three separable meanings.
questions.commonMistake: Swapping the second and third: ownership is privatisation; integration is globalisation.

questions.prompt: State two positive impacts of liberalisation on the Indian economy.
questions.answer: Freed from industrial licensing, firms could expand capacity and enter new lines in response to demand, so output grew and the shortages, queues and waiting lists of the licence era ended. Opening to imports and foreign investment introduced competition into markets that had faced none, and competition drove prices down while forcing quality up — the consumer changed from a supplicant waiting for allocation into a chooser comparing options. Foreign investment and technology inflows additionally let industry modernise without reinventing equipment and methods, raising productivity.
questions.explanation: Two impacts stated as mechanisms — control removed, possibility restored, effect shown — earn full marks; the consumer-side impact of competition is the strongest of the set to include.
questions.commonMistake: Restating the definition as the impact: “controls were removed” is meaning, not positive impact.

questions.prompt: Explain the meaning of globalisation and one positive impact of it.
questions.answer: Globalisation is the integration of a country’s economy with the world economy: freer flow of goods, services, capital, technology and people across borders so that producers, consumers and investors operate in one connected market rather than inside protected national ones. For India it meant cutting tariffs, abolishing quotas, welcoming foreign investment and letting Indian firms source and sell globally. One positive impact is the inflow of capital and technology: foreign investment supplements what domestic savings cannot fund alone and transfers production methods and quality standards that raise the productivity of Indian industry around them. Another is consumer welfare — imported and competitive domestic goods become cheaper and more varied, replacing the shortage economy’s queues with choice — while exports of software, textiles and pharmaceuticals earn foreign exchange and create employment.
questions.explanation: Meaning plus at least one impact stated as a mechanism earn full marks; including both the capital/technology and consumer effects makes the answer complete.
questions.commonMistake: Equating globalisation with imports alone — the flows of capital, technology and services are equally part of the definition.

questions.prompt: Explain the positive impacts of privatisation on the Indian economy.
questions.answer: Privatisation reduced the government’s role in production — disinvestment of public-sector equity, the opening of reserved areas to private firms, and commercial rather than administrative discipline for public undertakings that continued — and its positive impacts run on efficiency. Competition from private entrants forced public-sector units to cut costs and improve service: sectors like telecommunications and automobiles, once sole-source public monopolies, began responding to consumers once alternatives existed. Disinvestment brought professional management and private capital into firms whose boards had answered to departments, so decisions followed customers and performance instead of procedure. Entry into formerly reserved areas multiplied output, employment and choice — the consumer gained brands, features and prices where allocation had decided before. The fiscal burden eased as well: the government stopped accumulating bail-outs for loss-making units, freeing budget resources for infrastructure, health and education — state spending redirected from propping up firms to building the ground they stand on. The discipline of markets and shareholders made performance visible in a way departmental accounting never allowed, and firms that could not perform faced consequences rather than guarantees. The qualification matters: privatisation’s positive impacts depend on competition and regulation — a private monopoly without oversight replaces an efficient department with an expensive one — so the reform’s gains are properly claimed for the competition it introduces, not for private ownership in itself.
questions.explanation: Itemised impacts with mechanisms — competition, management, entry, fiscal redirection, visibility — plus the regulation caveat, together carry the full marks; the caveat shows the mechanism is understood rather than asserted.
questions.commonMistake: Listing only “efficiency increases” as if by magic, without saying which change produces it.

questions.prompt: How do liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation reinforce one another as a single package?
questions.answer: Each term answers a different part of the same problem, and each fails without the others — which is what makes the model a package. Liberalisation without globalisation would free Indian firms from domestic controls while shielding them from world competition: capacity could expand, but no external test would decide whether the expansion was efficient, so internal liberty could reproduce the licence era’s complacency with fewer forms to fill. Globalisation without liberalisation would open the borders while the licence regime still gated entry: imports would arrive and foreign capital would hover, but domestic firms could not respond to the new competition because expansion itself still required permission — the economy would face world prices with a structure frozen by administration. Privatisation without either would change owners without changing behaviour: a public monopoly sold intact becomes a private monopoly with the same untested position, since only competition disciplines ownership. Together the mechanisms compound. Licensing abolition let firms grow; foreign investment and technology supplied the capital and know-how to fill the new capacity; imports and new entrants determined which expansions deserved to survive; and the state, released from running firms, redirected resources towards the infrastructure, skills and regulation that all three need to function. The effects move in one direction at every stage — shortage replaced by choice, permission replaced by competition, isolation replaced by integration — and the reforms’ famous gains at the consumer’s counter, from one car model to a showroom of competitors, appeared only because all three moved at once. The conclusion the syllabus’s wording invites: meanings are three, impacts are three, and the mechanism is one — a coordinated substitution of market discipline for administrative discipline in domestic control, domestic ownership and foreign trade alike.
questions.explanation: The reinforcement answer must construct the three counterfactuals — each term alone and why it would fail — then show the compounding mechanism and the one-directional outcome; three parallel definitions with no interaction never earn the “package” marks.
questions.commonMistake: Defining the three again and calling the repetition reinforcement — the marks lie in the failure of each term practised alone.

questions.prompt: A critic says liberalisation benefited consumers but cost workers through casualisation and job insecurity. Assess both claims against the model’s positive impacts.
questions.answer: Both claims can be true at once, and assessing them requires holding the prescribed positive impacts and the labour-market evidence in the same frame. The consumer claim is well supported: competition from imports, new entrants and foreign investment ended the shortage economy, so prices fell relative to quality, variety expanded and the waiting lists for goods and telephones disappeared — liberalisation’s clearest impacts are visible at the counter precisely because the licence era had made the consumer a supplicant. The worker claim rests on a different mechanism. Faster growth with capital-intensive and skill-biased technology raises output per worker faster than headcount, so industries expanded while employing proportionately fewer people; alongside, the pressure to stay competitive pushed firms towards contract, casual and outsourced work that carries no security, leave or social insurance — employment grew but its form deteriorated, and casualisation converts the same reform’s efficiency gains into insecurity for those without scarce skills. Crucially, the two claims measure different things: consumer surplus on one side, employment quality and share of income on the other, and liberalisation maximised the first while leaving the second to regulation and labour policy that were built more slowly. The assessment therefore concludes conditionally. The positive impacts the syllabus asks for — expansion, competition, capital, technology, exports — are genuine and documented; so is the casualisation that accompanied them, and neither negates the other because the reform changed market structure while employment institutions adapted later. The policy reading follows: keep the competition that delivers the consumer impacts, and close the gap with the instruments that were not part of the package itself — enforceable labour protections, social security for casual workers, skill training matched to new demand, and employment-intensive growth in labour-using sectors. Reform judged honestly is not vindicated or condemned as a whole; its benefits are real, its distribution was underspecified, and completing the second half is the analytical task the criticism, at its best, is pointing to.
questions.explanation: Assessment marks require taking both claims seriously with mechanisms on each side, distinguishing the measures they use (consumer surplus vs employment quality), and reaching a conditional verdict with the policy completion — dismissing either side caps the answer.
questions.commonMistake: Defending the model by repeating positive impacts without engaging the worker claim, or accepting the critique by denying documented gains — both are one-sided and stay below the band.
